cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and release and push are both in your hand.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: There's a small growing thing you already keep — a plant on a sill, a pot on the step. Let its clock set the week. Water it when it wants, not when you think of it.
cells.core:
You know when to let a thing go and when to push it, and both come out of your hands without much noise. You've stood near enough collapses to tell which structures finish themselves and which want a shoulder. That's not a theory for you; it's callus.

Here, in a room where something is coming down fast, what's asked is lighter than the big gesture. Tend one small growing thing at its own pace, and find out what it actually needs by watching rather than deciding for it. Care that doesn't drain you comes from learning the thing's terms, not from holding on harder. You already lead by releasing. Let something small teach you the other half.
cells.sheetLine: You know what to let go of. Tend something small and learn it.
cells.verb: Laying your hand off the thing and letting it finish coming down
cells.place: A room where something that couldn't stand is coming apart quickly

cells.tense: You are braced already for how this comes down and what it will cost.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Take the crash you keep rehearsing — the falling-out, the loss, the ending — and write only what has actually happened so far, in order, no feeling words. Read the page back once.
cells.core:
You govern by knowing what a thing costs before you spend it, and the spending is going into a wreck that hasn't finished arriving. Something is coming apart, and your mind is already at the far end of it, holding a moment that can't be written yet. The push is landing somewhere the situation hasn't reached.

Put it on paper instead. Just what has happened, in order, stripped of how it all feels. Most of what you're bracing against won't be in the written record, and the part that is turns out to be something a person can carry rather than forecast. Rigour serves you here better than dread. You know how to hold heavy things. Hold this one at its real size.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that already closed behind you.
cells.act: lay the one step you can see, solidly
cells.ask: Take the next ordinary task that is sitting there waiting — the call, the box, the form — and do that one thing slowly and completely, then set it down. Nothing beyond it.
cells.core:
The release you carry hasn't come back yet. Where something was coming apart, you stayed at the edge of it and your heat went out with the thing that left. You're holding a doorway with nobody in it, and the part of you that finishes things has stepped away.

You get it back through your hands, not your head. Do one plain task, slowly and completely, the way a builder sets a stone and checks it sits level. Then stop. Seeing the whole structure isn't required to lay one course of it. That single course is enough to bring the energy back through what's been starved, and the rest of the sequence shows itself once you're standing on something solid.

cells.tense: The letting-go is already happening and you're not counting it as yours.
cells.act: learn how it grows by tending it
cells.ask: A routine, a small system, a person's habit stays alive because you keep feeding it. Tend it once this week, then write one line: this runs because you hold it.
cells.core:
You've been the one releasing what was done — quietly, on time, without ceremony — and if anyone asked, you'd say it happened by itself. Several things near you are lighter because somebody knew when to let go. That somebody is you, and it isn't being counted.

The way in is smaller than what you do. Tend one modest thing that stays alive because you keep it so, then put the plain fact of it on paper: this runs because you hold it. You'll feel how strange the claim sits. That strangeness is the gap. Care that doesn't exhaust begins with knowing whose hands the care is in, and yours have been the hands the whole time, working while their owner was looking elsewhere.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that these structures are 'false' — the record says only that things built on premises that couldn't hold come down fast and that this can feel like liberation, not that what is falling is wrong or deserves to fall. A reader could reasonably say the letting-go in Too Much is just exhaustion, or that the pull-back in Too Little was fear, neither of which the record supports. The asks survive being wrong: each is one act on a real thing in front of them, useful whichever way my read sits. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any line that makes the collapse sound like a verdict on what they built; it has been cut.
